doc.title: Scott Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe,Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Getting into bass saxophone: grandfather's alto and the school's bass sax
summary: He started on his grandfather's alto, moved to baritone, discovered a high school bass sax, and eventually acquired and restored one.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: You’ve become quite a woodwind specialist and do things that not that many other people do, like the bass saxophone and so forth. How did you get into that low end of the spectrum?
Well the bass sax is a passion of mine. I have to say it’s probably my favorite of the saxophones, although I can actually do more on the tenor for now.
When you say “do more” do you mean play more?

I can be more flexible and play in more situations. I have better range and better control. But I’ve taken the bass sax to where I can feel very comfortable on it in almost any situation. And I hope to take it to the level where it will be just another tenor for me, but of course an octave lower. In answer to your question about getting into the bass sax, I started on alto. I started on my grandfather’s alto, which I still play today, it’s a Conn that he bought in 1927 and he played with a little dance band when he was in school, along with my grandmother, she played the violin. And I dearly wish I had a picture of them in that group but none exist. Then I switched to baritone, because baritone was needed in the high school — or not in high school, in the junior high band. I went from alto right to baritone. It wasn’t until high school that I started playing tenor. I thought the baritone was a huge, monster instrument, and then somebody told me, “You know there’s one even bigger and that’s bass saxophone.” I said, “Come on.” “No there is, and Herndan High School has one.” And I didn’t believe it but I finally got my first chance to go into Herndan High School and I saw this thing in the band room and it was just amazing to me. So I started carrying it home and borrowing it and playing on it. The band director was very nice, he let me take it home, and I walked back and forth to school and I was a little gangly little kid carrying this incredibly heavy thing in a wooden case, carrying it through these fields, which are now all built up unfortunately. But I remember the handle was on the sloping part of the case and it was a hard, kind of a sharp edged handle, and it was on the slope, so all the weight was pulled down right into this part of my hand like this, and it was agony. But man, when I got that thing home, I sure had a ball with it. © Hamilton Fillius Archive -5-
You were paying some dues just getting it home.

Oh, boy, I said, this is really something. And I dreamed of someday having one. And I finally did get one. It’s a long story but there was one at another high school that was completely banged up and unplayable and I had seen it there once. And so after I got to college I got thinking about it and I said I want that horn. I started calling down there and asking about it. And they said, “Oh it belongs to the school and we can’t part with it” and all that. But just to shorten the story, after twelve years, the guy retired and a new band director came in and he said we can’t use this thing, we’re going to put it on an obsolete list and then we can get rid of it. So I went down and I made a special trip down there to see it and he got it out and it was all old and a couple of parts were missing and he says, “Oh gee, I didn’t realize it was that bad,” he says, “Well if you donate fifty bucks to the band department, we’ll give you the horn.” So I got this horn that I restored, and I made the keys for it and everything.
No kidding. You made it yourself?

Yeah. I knew I was going to get one someday. I had already written a piece for it called “Rapture of the Deep.” And sometimes that seems to be a good way to get an instrument I need, if I write music for it, then it sets up a kind of gravitational field and eventually I think it will come to me.
